turn_text: So for folks who may not know you, tell us a little bit about yourself.

Sure, my name is Mary Peltola. I was born and raised in Bethel along the Cusco Coom River, actually three little villages outside of Bethel. I grew up commercial fishing for kings at the beginning of the season, and then chums right after that, and reds, and then we finished up with silvers. And my family also had a tender boat operation. My dad ran a tender boat. And then my sister and I were captains of a commercial fishing boat different times over the years. So that's how I was raised. I worked for Fish and Game when I was in college. I imagined I was going to become a teacher, and so I went to college teacher training. And as it happened, I did a legislative internship at the Capitol in Juneau in 1996, and really was drawn to public policy in the public process. turn_text: Well, primarily my interest was on reauthorizing Magnuson Stevens Act. I think everyone recognizes that we are living in a very different paradigm than the one we had before 2010. The Magnuson Stevens Act hasn't been reauthorized since 2007. And we just have a real different ocean productivity level. We have a different level of abundance. I would say we don't have the abundance that we're accustomed to as Alaskans. And that's presenting a myriad of food security issues on the West Coast of Alaska. And it's been surprising to me how little that's been talked about and how little action has been taken on that. And it's really been status quo. We've been in this low abundance paradigm for 13 summers now. And we don't see traction in terms of policy or really investing in science. And there seems to be an attitude at the policy level that until we know why these things are happening, we can't do anything. And I believe we need to take precautionary management and be changing the way we're doing things while we're finding out what the causes of these problems are. turn_text: What are some of the other key issues that you'd like to address as a congressman?

Well, I would love to serve all Alaskans, regardless of party. I am running as a Democrat. However, folks who worked with me in Juneau will be the first to tell you I'm very nonpartisan. I helped reestablish the Bush Caucus, which was a coalition of 10 out of 40 on the House side. of off-road system legislators. And the Bush Caucus was almost every year, five Republicans and five Democrats. And we didn't just focus on our regions or off-road system. What often, almost all the time, what is good for a rural area is good for the whole state. Working in a bipartisan way, I think it's really important in Alaska as well as across the states that we Find a way to get away from this hyper-partisanship. I think it's very toxic and I think it doesn't help us move forward. I think it really takes us backwards and I would certainly like to be part of that effort. It's just really important that we focus on policies, we focus on making sure everyone is at the table. One of the things that I am finding across America is regardless of what your background is, everyone is feeling disenfranchised, everyone is feeling forgotten and isolated. And I think that some of the dialogue has been about groups that are typically seen as minorities, not being at the table, but I think 100% of us feel that we have been minimized and forgotten.
